findings.title: Adding an abstract SPI method breaks existing custom grant providers
findings.body: `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` is an extension interface, and adding `getShortcut()` as an abstract method makes all already-built third-party implementations binary incompatible. During startup `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` calls this method on every grant factory, so an extension compiled against the previous interface will fail with `AbstractMethodError` (and source implementations will no longer compile) rather than allowing the server to start. Provide a default implementation/fallback for providers that do not supply a shortcut, or introduce a compatible optional interface.

findings.title: Grant shortcut contract permits values the encoder cannot decode
findings.body: The new API documentation says a shortcut is usually three letters, but `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider` unconditionally parses exactly two characters for the grant shortcut and requires the entire encoded context to be six characters. A custom factory following this documented contract with a three-character shortcut will successfully issue IDs such as `onrtabc:<uuid>`, but `getTokenContextFromTokenId` will reject them as malformed. The factory must validate and enforce exactly two-character shortcuts (including dynamic providers), or the encoding needs a length-delimited format and matching documentation.

findings.title: rawTokenId is not null-checked
findings.body: The constructor checks `grantType` twice; the second check has the raw-token error message but does not validate `rawTokenId`. A caller of this public SPI can construct a context with a null raw ID, and `encodeTokenId` will then produce an ID ending in the literal string `null` instead of failing fast. Validate `rawTokenId` in the second `requireNonNull` call.

findings.title: Access-token ID matcher does not verify the expected grant shortcut
findings.body: The matcher extracts `substring(3, 5)`, although the grant occupies positions 4-5 in the six-character prefix, and then returns false when that extracted value equals the expected shortcut. Consequently, a token with a wrong grant shortcut normally passes the matcher, while certain matching values fail. The updated event assertions therefore do not test the grant encoding they were added for; compare `substring(4, 6)` to the expected shortcut and fail when they differ.
